**On Meanders**

If you give a river a flat, soft floodplain and enough time, it will refuse to run straight. This seems almost perverse. Water wants to go downhill; the shortest path downhill is a straight line; and yet nearly every mature river on Earth wanders across its valley in loops so regular they look designed. Seen from above, the Mississippi near Greenville, the Amazon near Iquitos, and a nameless creek in a Wyoming meadow all draw the same shape—just at wildly different scales. The ratio between the wavelength of a meander and the width of the channel hovers around ten or eleven, whether the channel is three meters wide or three kilometers. Rivers, it turns out, are not improvising. They are playing a tune they can't help knowing.

I find this oddly consoling, and I want to try to say why.

The mechanism is not mysterious once you see it. A perfectly straight channel is unstable. Any tiny irregularity—a fallen log, a patch of harder clay, a slightly deeper pool—pushes the current toward one bank. Where the water runs faster along the outside of the nascent curve, it scours the bank away; where it slows along the inside, it drops its sediment. The curve deepens. The faster outer water, now flung by the bend, crosses over and slams into the opposite bank a little farther downstream, starting the next curve in the other direction. So the smallest deviation from straightness amplifies itself into a sinuous wave that propagates downstream and, over centuries, migrates across the whole valley. Nothing about it was decided. The river simply cannot stay straight, in the way a pencil balanced on its point cannot stay upright.

What is remarkable is the *regularity*. Chaos ought to produce a mess, and instead it produces something close to a sine curve. In the 1960s, the hydrologist Luna Leopold and the physicist Walter Langbein argued that meander shapes are the curves that minimize the total variance in direction change along the path—the "sine-generated curve," the same shape a thin steel strip takes when you push its ends together. It is the curve of least work. The river, without any intention, finds the path along which its turning is most evenly distributed. It spreads its effort. It avoids sharp corners not because corners are ugly but because they are expensive.

I think about this whenever someone says that freedom means the absence of constraint. The river is about as free as a physical system gets. No one dug its bed. It has no destination beyond the sea and no plan for getting there. Yet the moment it is released onto the plain, it begins to make the same shape every other free river makes. Its freedom is not the freedom to do anything—it is the freedom to discover, by trial, the one form its situation allows. Constraint and liberty here are not opposites. The constraint (gravity, viscosity, the erodibility of silt) is what gives the liberty something to become.

There is also the matter of oxbows. When a meander loop grows so extreme that its two ends nearly touch, a flood will eventually punch through the narrow neck and the river will abandon the loop entirely, straightening for a moment before it begins to wander again. The severed loop becomes an oxbow lake, a crescent of still water gradually filling with reeds and silt and then with willows and then with nothing recognizable at all, just a slight curve in the color of a wheat field visible only from a plane. The floodplains of great rivers are littered with these ghost channels, thousands of them, layered over each other like handwriting on a page that has been used again and again. The Mississippi's plain, in the right light, is an archive of every place the river has ever been.

I like that the river's past is not erased but merely demoted. The current channel is only the most recent draft. The old drafts are still there, holding water in wet years, growing different trees, shaping where towns were built and where roads had to bend. A landscape is a memory made of dirt.

Engineers spent much of the twentieth century trying to talk rivers out of meandering. They straightened them, lined them with concrete, cut off the oxbows, all in the name of flood control and navigation. The results were instructive. A straightened river runs faster, which means it erodes faster, which means it digs its own bed deeper, lowers the water table around it, undermines its banks, and delivers flood pulses downstream with greater violence. Wetlands that had depended on the slow spill of a wandering channel dried up. Fish that spawned in the quiet pools on the inside of bends found no quiet pools. The Kissimmee River in Florida was carved into a canal in the 1960s and has been, since the 1990s, laboriously re-bent at great cost—the meanders re-excavated, the canal filled in, the river coaxed back into the shape it would have taken anyway if we had left it alone. There is a lesson there about the difference between forcing a form and permitting one.

I don't want to overload the metaphor. A river is not a person and a floodplain is not a life. But I notice that when I try to think about how anything develops—a friendship, a piece of writing, a career, a language—the straight line is always the fantasy and the meander is always the truth. The direct route, the one that looks efficient from above, turns out to be unstable the moment it meets any real resistance. What actually happens is that something small deflects us, the deflection amplifies, we swing wide, we cross back over, and we discover after the fact that our wandering had a wavelength.

And the loops we abandon don't vanish. They sit there in the plain, filling slowly with reeds, changing the color of the fields.
